sections.text:
Moses is old, and he is standing on the plains of Moab, speaking to a people about to cross into the land without him. These are his last words, and he does not hurry them. In a series of speeches he retells the journey, restates the law for a generation about to enter the land, and sets before them blessing and curse, life and death.

At the heart of it is a call that sits at the heart of the book: “Hear, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one.” And then: “You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.” (6:4 and 5)

The book closes with Moses climbing Mount Nebo. The LORD shows him the whole land, and tells him, “you shall not go over there.” Moses dies in the land of Moab, and “no man knows where his tomb is to this day.”

The name means second law, in the sense of the law given again. Many scholars note that the book is shaped like the treaties ancient kings made with their peoples. Tradition links it with Moses. Many scholars think it reached its final form later, and connect it with the reform of King Josiah in the seventh century before Christ.

Deuteronomy is one of the books the New Testament quotes most. Jesus answers each temptation in the wilderness with words from it, and names its call to love God as the greatest commandment.

Its teaching that faithfulness leads to life and unfaithfulness to loss shapes the books from Joshua to Kings. Christians read its promises and warnings in the light of the new covenant in Christ.

A man is looking back. Moses stands beyond the Jordan in the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, and begins to speak to all Israel. These are the words of a leader who knows he will not cross the river.

He goes back to Horeb, where the LORD told the people they had stayed long enough at that mountain. He remembers sharing the load by appointing wise men as captains and judges, and telling them not to show partiality, because the judgment is God's.

Then he comes to Kadesh Barnea. Twelve spies went in, brought back fruit, and said it was a good land. But the people would not go up. They murmured in their tents and said the LORD hated them. Moses told them not to be afraid and reminded them that the LORD carried them as a man carries his son. They did not believe.

The LORD swore that none of that generation would see the land, except Caleb. Moses himself is told he will not enter. When they tried to fight on their own, they were beaten back.

Deuteronomy is presented as Moses' farewell speeches on the plains of Moab. Tradition links the book to Moses, and many scholars think its final form is later. He is speaking to the children of those who left Egypt, retelling the story so they will choose differently. The Kadesh events are first told in Numbers 13 and 14. Here they are told in Moses' own voice, as a warning from one who was there.

For many days the people walked in circles around Mount Seir. Then the LORD said: you have encircled this mountain long enough. Turn northward.

The next part is a lesson in borders. Edom belongs to the children of Esau, Moab to the children of Lot, and Ammon too. Israel is told not to contend with them or take any of their land, and to pay for food and water. The text says that for forty years the LORD has been with Israel, and they lacked nothing.

The long wait ends. It took thirty-eight years from Kadesh Barnea to the brook Zered, until all the men of war were gone, as the LORD swore.

Then comes Sihon, king of Heshbon. Moses sent him words of peace and asked to pass through. Sihon refused, and the chapter says the LORD had hardened his spirit. Israel defeated him and utterly destroyed every inhabited city, with women and little ones.

Moses is still retelling the journey, now covering the years after Kadesh. The land of Edom, Moab and Ammon is treated as given by the LORD to other peoples, so Israel's own claim is limited to what it was given. The accounts of Sihon and Og are first told in Numbers 21. The destruction of whole cities is the most difficult part of this chapter, and Jewish and Christian readers have long struggled with it.

The road turns north, and a giant stands in the way. Og, king of Bashan, comes out with all his people to battle at Edrei. The LORD tells Moses not to fear him, because he is already delivered into their hand. Israel takes sixty cities. The text adds an odd detail: Og's iron bedstead was nine cubits long.

Moses then recalls how he divided the new land among Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh. Their men would cross the Jordan armed in front of their brothers, while wives, children and livestock stayed in the cities.

The chapter ends quietly. Moses begged the LORD to let him cross and see the good land beyond the Jordan. The answer is no: that is enough, speak no more of this. He may climb Pisgah and look in every direction with his own eyes, but Joshua will lead the people over. Moses is told to encourage him. So they stayed in the valley near Beth Peor.

This is the third chapter of Moses' opening speech on the plains of Moab. He is giving his people the history that leads to the moment they are in. Og and Sihon were told in Numbers 21, and the arrangement with the eastern tribes in Numbers 32. The personal plea of Moses is one of the most human moments in the book, and it is linked back to the events at Meribah in Numbers 20.

Moses turns from history to a plea. Listen, Israel, to the statutes and ordinances I teach you, so that you may live and go in and possess the land. Do not add to the word, and do not take away from it.

He asks them to remember Horeb, the day the mountain burned with fire to the heart of the sky, and the LORD spoke out of the fire. They heard a voice of words, but saw no form. Because they saw no form, they are warned never to make an image of anything, nor to worship sun, moon or stars.

Moses says he himself must die in this land, and he warns that if Israel forgets and corrupts itself, they will be scattered among the nations. But from there, if they seek the LORD with all their heart and soul, they will find him. The LORD is a merciful God who will not forget the covenant.

No other people ever heard the voice of God out of the fire and lived. Three cities of refuge are set apart east of the Jordan.

Moses is speaking to the generation that stood at Horeb as children or was born after it. His main concern is faithfulness to the one God without images. The warning of scattering is read by many Jews and Christians as looking ahead to the exile, and the promise of return is read alongside Deuteronomy 30. The statement that the LORD is God and there is no one else is basic to later Jewish and Christian teaching on one God.

Moses calls all Israel together and says something surprising. The LORD did not make this covenant with our fathers, but with us, even us who are all here alive today. The mountain is not only in the past.

He recalls the day at Horeb, when the people were afraid of the fire and he stood between them and the LORD. Then the Ten Commandments are given, beginning with “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.” No other gods. No carved image. Do not misuse the name. Keep the Sabbath, and the text ties it to the memory of slavery in Egypt, so that servants and animals rest as well. Honor father and mother. “You shall not murder.” No adultery, theft, false testimony or coveting.

The people, terrified by the voice from the fire, ask Moses to go near and hear for them. The LORD says they have spoken well and wishes they would always have such a heart.

The Ten Commandments were first told in Exodus 20, and here Moses repeats them to a new generation on the plains of Moab. A few details differ from Exodus, such as the reason given for the Sabbath, and readers have noticed and discussed them. Jewish, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions divide and number the commandments in somewhat different ways. The commandments are read as the heart of the covenant.

Moses gives the people the words that Jews call the Shema. “Hear, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one.” Then comes the command that follows: love the LORD your God with all your heart, soul and might.

These words are not meant to stay in a scroll. They are to be on the heart, taught diligently to children, and talked about sitting at home, walking on the road, lying down and rising up. They are bound as a sign on the hand and frontlets between the eyes, and written on the door posts and gates.

Moses looks ahead to a land of houses they did not build and vineyards they did not plant, and he warns about forgetting the LORD when they are full. When a son asks what these laws mean, the answer is a story: we were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt, and the LORD brought us out.

They are told not to tempt the LORD as they did at Massah.

Moses is still speaking to Israel on the plains of Moab, now explaining what the commandments of chapter 5 ask of daily life. Jewish tradition has made verses 4 to 9 a daily prayer, and some Jews still wear and mount these words in small boxes. Jesus quotes the command to love God in Matthew 22, Mark 12 and Luke 10. Christians and Jews read the physical signs in different ways, some literally and others figuratively.

Moses looks ahead to a land full of nations, seven of them, greater and mightier than Israel. He tells the people what to do when the LORD delivers them up: utterly destroy them, make no covenant, show no mercy, and make no marriages with them. Break down their altars, dash their pillars, burn their engraved images. The reason given is that their sons would be turned to other gods.

Then the chapter pauses on a surprise. Israel is a holy people, chosen not because they were many, for they were the fewest of all peoples, but because the LORD loves them and keeps his oath. He is the faithful God who keeps covenant to a thousand generations.

Moses promises blessing for obedience and warns against fear: remember what the LORD did to Pharaoh. The nations will be cast out little by little.

Moses is preparing a nation for entering Canaan, and the language of total destruction is some of the hardest in the Bible. Many scholars note that such language was common in the ancient world and may be partly formal, and some point out that later books show the peoples were not wiped out. This text has been misused to justify violence against groups in later history, and Jewish and Christian readers have sharply rejected that use. Compare Deuteronomy 20 and Joshua 9 to 11.

Remember the way. Moses asks Israel to look back on forty years in the wilderness, and he says what they were for: that the LORD might humble them, test them, and know what was in their heart.

He tells them what hunger taught. The LORD fed them with manna, which neither they nor their fathers had known, so that they would learn “man does not live by bread only” in the wilderness. Their clothing did not wear out, and their feet did not swell. As a man disciplines his son, so the LORD disciplines them.

Then Moses paints the good land ahead: brooks and springs, wheat, barley, vines, figs, pomegranates, olives and honey, with iron in the stones and copper in the hills. But he sees the danger of plenty. When you have eaten and built fine houses and your silver is multiplied, do not say that your own power got you this wealth. It is the LORD who gives power to get wealth.

Forgetting him and following other gods would end in perishing.

Moses is addressing the people just before the Jordan crossing. The wilderness is remembered here as a school as well as a hardship. Jesus quotes the line about bread when he is tempted in the wilderness in Matthew 4 and Luke 4. The warning about prosperity is a theme that appears across the book and again in the prophets.

Israel is about to cross the Jordan to face cities fortified up to the sky and the sons of Anak, and Moses tells them how it will go: the LORD himself goes over before them as a devouring fire.

Then he turns the story against any pride. Do not say the LORD brings you in because of your righteousness. It is because of the wickedness of these nations, and to keep his oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. You are a stiff-necked people.

He proves it with a memory. At Horeb he stayed on the mountain forty days and nights while the LORD wrote the tablets. Meanwhile the people made a molded calf. Moses came down, threw the two tablets, and broke them before their eyes. Then he fell down before the LORD for another forty days and nights and prayed, and the LORD listened.

His prayer rests on the LORD's own name: they are your people and your inheritance.

This is part of Moses' long address on the plains of Moab, retelling the golden calf of Exodus 32 to 34 from his own point of view. Notice that the reason given for the conquest is the wickedness of the nations and the LORD's promise, not Israel's merit. The statement about the nations' wickedness is a hard claim, and some readers have misused it. The prayer of Moses is also remembered in Psalm 106.

After the breaking comes the mending. The LORD tells Moses to cut two new stone tablets like the first and to make an ark of wood. He writes the same words on them, the ten commandments, and Moses puts them in the ark, where they remain.

A short note about the journey and the death of Aaron at Moserah is set in parentheses, followed by the setting apart of the tribe of Levi to carry the ark. The LORD himself is their inheritance.

Then the center of the chapter: “what does the LORD your God require of you,” The answer is to fear him, walk in his ways, love him, and serve him with all your heart and soul. All heaven and earth belong to him, yet he set his love on the fathers. Moses says to circumcise the foreskin of your heart.

The LORD does not respect persons or take bribes. He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the foreigner. So love the foreigner, for you were foreigners in Egypt.

Moses is continuing his retelling of Horeb. The second tablets follow the broken ones of Deuteronomy 9, and the story is first told in Exodus 34. The phrase about the circumcision of the heart appears again in Deuteronomy 30, Jeremiah 4 and Romans 2. The command to love the foreigner is a clear ethical center in the middle of a book that also contains hard laws.

Moses speaks to the generation that saw it. Your children have not seen the discipline of the LORD, but your eyes have seen his great work: the signs in Egypt, the army drowned in the Red Sea, and the earth opening to swallow Dathan and Abiram.

Then he describes the land ahead, and how different it is from Egypt, where the seed was watered by foot like a garden of herbs. This land is one of hills and valleys that drinks rain from the sky, a land the LORD cares for, with his eyes on it from the beginning of the year to the end.

The rain, though, depends on the people. If they listen and love, the early and latter rain will come, and they will eat and be full. If their hearts are deceived and they serve other gods, the sky will shut up.

The words are to be laid up in the heart, taught to children, and written on door posts. Moses sets before them a blessing and a curse, to be proclaimed at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.

Moses is closing the opening part of his speeches before the detailed laws begin in chapter 12. The contrast between Egypt's irrigated fields and Canaan's rain-fed hills sets up the idea that the land's fruitfulness is tied to faithfulness. The blessing and curse on Gerizim and Ebal are carried out in Joshua 8. This chapter repeats the instructions about teaching children from Deuteronomy 6.

Moses stands on the edge of a land full of other people's shrines, and his first instruction is to tear them down. Altars, pillars, Asherah poles and carved images on every high hill and under every green tree are to go, and their names with them. Israel is not to treat the LORD that way.

Instead there will be one place that the LORD chooses to put his name. Offerings, tithes, vows and firstborn animals are to be brought there, and the people are to eat before the LORD and rejoice, sons, daughters, servants and the Levite together.

Ordinary meat is a different matter. Within their own gates they may eat as their appetite wishes, but never the blood, which is poured out like water, for the blood is the life. Moses closes with a warning not to ask how the nations served their gods, and not to add to his words or take away from them.

Chapter 12 opens the long section of laws, usually called the Deuteronomic Code, that runs to chapter 26. Moses is speaking to the generation about to enter Canaan. Many scholars think the focus on one chosen place explains why later passages, such as 1 Kings 8, centre worship on Jerusalem, though the chapter itself never names a city. The harsh language about the nations is tied here to their worship practices, and it should be read with the hard texts of chapter 20.

What if the miracle is real? Moses begins with the hardest case. A prophet or a dreamer of dreams gives a sign, the sign comes true, and then he says, Let us go after other gods. Israel is told not to listen. The LORD is testing whether they love him with all their heart and soul.

Then the circle tightens. The same temptation may come from a brother, a son, a daughter, the wife of your bosom, or a friend as close as your own soul. Israel is to give no consent and show no pity, and such a person is to be stoned to death.

Last comes a whole city led astray. Israel must inquire and investigate diligently. If the report is certain, the city is to be struck with the sword and burned, a heap forever, and nothing of the devoted thing is to cling to anyone's hand.

This chapter reads like the treaties of its day, where loyalty to the one sovereign is the heart of the agreement, and here the sovereign is the LORD who brought Israel out of Egypt. These are some of the most severe laws in the Bible. Readers have long asked how they were applied, and the call to investigate carefully in verse 14 matters to that question. Christians and Jews read such laws differently, and many stress that the New Testament never calls for this kind of penalty.

You are the children of the LORD your God. Moses begins with belonging, and then shows what belonging looks like on the table and at the grave. Israel is not to cut themselves or shave their foreheads for the dead, because they are a holy people, chosen for his own possession.

Then comes the list of food. Animals with a split hoof that chew the cud may be eaten, and the camel, the hare and the pig may not. Fish with fins and scales are allowed. A long run of birds is named as forbidden, from the eagle to the bat. Nothing that dies of itself is to be eaten, and a young goat is not to be boiled in its mother's milk.

The chapter ends with the tithe. It is to be eaten before the LORD in a joyful feast, or turned into money if the way is long. Every third year it is stored at home for the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow.

The food laws here run parallel to those in Leviticus 11. Scholars and traditions explain them in different ways, as marks of Israel's distinctness, as signs of order in creation, or in other ways, and the text gives only one reason, that Israel is holy to the LORD. Most Christians hold that the New Testament sets these rules aside, as in Mark 7 and Acts 10, while Jewish tradition keeps them. The care for the poor in the closing verses ties the chapter to chapter 15.

Every seventh year, debts are to be cancelled. Moses says it plainly: no creditor may press a neighbor or a brother, because the LORD's release has been proclaimed. A foreigner may still be asked to pay.

The chapter then looks at the human heart behind the law. Do not harden your heart, and do not shut your hand. Beware the quiet thought that the year of release is near, so why lend at all. Open your hand and give, and do not be grieved when you do. Verse 11 admits that the poor will never cease out of the land, and for that very reason the command is to open the hand.

Then comes the Hebrew servant, set free in the seventh year and sent away with gifts from flock, threshing floor and wine press. Remember that you were a slave in Egypt. A servant who loves the household may choose to stay, and the chapter closes with the rules for the firstborn of the herd.

Moses speaks of the sabbatical year as a way to keep poverty from becoming permanent, and the memory of Egypt is the reason he gives. Verses 4 and 11 sit side by side, one hoping for no poor among them and one admitting that there will be, and readers have long noted the tension. The servitude here is not the same as slavery in later empires, but it is still hard to read, and the text sets limits on it. See Leviticus 25 and Exodus 21 for related laws.

Three times a year the whole nation is to come before the LORD, and Moses walks through the calendar. First the Passover, in the month when the LORD brought them out of Egypt by night. Unleavened bread is the bread of affliction, eaten in haste as they once left, so that they remember the day all their lives.

Seven weeks after the first sickle touches the grain comes the feast of weeks, and then the feast of booths after the harvest. The joy is wide. Sons, daughters, servants, the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow are all to rejoice together. No one is to come empty, and each gives as able.

Then the chapter turns to justice. Judges and officers are to be set in every gate. They must not pervert justice or show partiality, and no bribe is allowed, for it blinds the eyes of the wise. Follow what is altogether just, and do not plant an Asherah beside the altar.

These three feasts are also listed in Exodus 23 and Leviticus 23, and later Judaism and Christianity kept their memory in Passover, Pentecost and Sukkot, and in the Christian reading of Easter and Pentecost. Here the stress falls on one place of worship and on the joy that includes people with no land. The sudden turn to judges shows how worship and fairness belong together in the book. Compare Deuteronomy 17 and Amos 5.

The chapter begins with a small, sharp rule: do not offer the LORD an ox or sheep with a defect. It then moves to a serious charge of serving other gods. The case must be investigated diligently. No one may be put to death on the word of one witness, and the witnesses are to cast the first stones.

For matters too hard for local judges, there is a higher court at the place the LORD chooses, with the Levitical priests and the judge of those days. Their verdict is to be followed without turning right or left.

Then Moses looks ahead to a day when Israel says, I will set a king over me, like all the nations. If they do, the king must be chosen by the LORD and be one of their own brothers. He is not to multiply horses, wives, silver or gold, and he must write his own copy of this law and read it all his life, so his heart is not lifted above his brothers.

The king in verses 14 to 20 is not commanded but permitted, and the text sets limits on him from the start. Many scholars see this passage as a lens for reading the books of Samuel and Kings, where kings such as Solomon gather horses, wives and gold. The rule of two or three witnesses is repeated in Deuteronomy 19 and is quoted in the New Testament, as in Matthew 18. Verses 2 to 7 are among the hard laws of the book.

The Levites have no land. Moses says it plainly: the LORD is their inheritance. They live from the offerings of the people, a share of the sacrifices and the first fruits of grain, wine, oil and fleece.

Then he warns about the land they are about to enter. The nations there burn their children in fire, and they use divination, fortune telling, sorcery, charms, mediums and the calling up of the dead. All of this is an abomination to the LORD, and Israel is to be blameless.

In its place the LORD will raise up a prophet from among their brothers, like Moses. It goes back to Horeb, where the people begged never to hear the voice or see the fire again, and the LORD said they had spoken well. He will put his words in the prophet's mouth. The chapter ends with a test: if what a prophet says in the LORD's name does not come to pass, the LORD has not spoken it, and the people need not fear him.

Verse 15 is among the best known passages of Deuteronomy. Jewish tradition has often read the promised prophet as the line of prophets that followed Moses. The New Testament applies it to Jesus in Acts 3 and Acts 7, and many Christians read it both ways. The test in verses 21 and 22 is balanced by chapter 13, where a true sign is not enough if the message turns people from the LORD. The ban on child sacrifice is repeated in Leviticus 18.

Picture two men chopping wood in a forest. One swings an ax, and the head slips from the handle and strikes his neighbor dead. Moses uses this scene to show what the cities of refuge are for. Three cities are to be set apart, with roads prepared, so that a man who killed without hatred can flee there and live, and not be caught by the avenger of blood while his anger is hot.

If the LORD enlarges Israel's border, three more are to be added. But a murderer who lies in wait does not find safety there, and the elders are to hand him over.

The chapter closes with fairness in court. Do not move a neighbor's landmark. One witness is not enough, and two or three establish a matter. A false witness is to receive what he planned to do to his brother. The measure is life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth.

The cities of refuge are also described in Numbers 35 and Joshua 20, where the names of six cities are given. The law separates accidental killing from murder, which was an important step in a world of family revenge. The phrase eye for eye is used here for false witnesses, a limit on punishment, and Jesus refers to it in Matthew 5. Jews and Christians have long read it as a rule of proportion and not a demand for revenge.

Horses, chariots and a people more numerous than you. Moses starts from the moment of fear. Israel is not to be afraid, because the LORD who brought them out of Egypt is with them. A priest speaks to the army before the fight: Do not let your heart faint, for the LORD goes with you to fight for you.

Then the officers speak, and the exemptions are startling. Anyone who has built a house and not dedicated it, planted a vineyard and not eaten from it, or promised to marry and not yet married may go home. So may the fearful and faint-hearted.

For a distant city, Israel must first offer peace. If it refuses and falls, the men are struck down, and the women, children and goods are taken. For the cities of the Hittite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite and Jebusite, nothing that breathes is to live, so Israel does not learn their abominations. Even in a siege, fruit trees are not to be cut down.

This is one of the hardest chapters in the Bible, and the text says what it says. Readers differ on how to take it. Some see a command limited to one time and one set of peoples, some note that the book of Joshua describes a conquest less total than these words, and some, such as many Jewish and Christian writers, have warned against using it to justify any later violence. The rules about peace offers, exemptions and trees are unusual for the ancient world. See Joshua 6 and 11.

A man is found dead in a field, and no one knows who struck him. Moses gives the nearest city a ceremony. The elders take a heifer that has never worked, break its neck in an unplowed valley with running water, wash their hands over it and say, Our hands have not shed this blood. They ask the LORD to forgive his people and not leave innocent blood among them.

Then come several family cases, each hard to read. A soldier who desires a captive woman must give her a month to mourn her parents before marriage, and may not sell her if he later loses interest. A man with two wives must give the firstborn his double portion even if the mother is the one he does not love. A son who is stubborn and rebellious, a glutton and a drunkard, is brought by his parents to the elders, and the city is to stone him.

The chapter ends with a body hanging on a tree, which must be buried the same day, for the land is not to be defiled.

The chapter shows how Israel handled guilt for unsolved crimes, and why. It also includes laws that are hard to read now, on captive women and on a rebellious son. Many scholars think the rebellious son law was meant to set a high bar, since both parents had to bring the charge. Paul quotes verse 23 in Galatians 3 when he speaks of Christ bearing a curse, and John 19 notes that Jesus was taken down before night.

Moses opens with a lost ox. If you see your brother's ox or sheep go astray, do not hide yourself from it. Bring it back, keep it at your house until he comes looking, and do the same with a donkey, a garment or any lost thing. The same goes for an animal fallen on the road. Help lift it up.

The chapter is a collection of small laws that treat daily life as a place of duty. A mother bird is not to be taken with her young. A new house must have a railing around the roof, so that no one falls and brings blood on the house. Fields, plows and cloth are not to be mixed, and tassels are to be sewn on a cloak.

Then come hard cases about sexuality and marriage. A man who falsely slanders his bride is fined and may never divorce her. A woman who is attacked in the open country is declared to have no sin worthy of death, since no one was there to save her. Other cases call for stoning.

The cases on sexual conduct are some of the hardest in the book. They assume a world where a daughter's marriage involved her family and the town elders, and they raise real questions about justice for women that readers have long debated. Note that verses 25 to 27 clearly protect the victim of an attack. The cloak fringes are explained in Numbers 15. Verse 5, on clothing, is read in different ways by different traditions.

Who may come into the assembly of the LORD, and who may not? Moses gives a list that is hard to read. A man who has been emasculated, a person born of a forbidden union, an Ammonite or a Moabite are all kept out, the last because they did not meet Israel with bread and water and hired Balaam to curse them. But the LORD turned the curse into a blessing, because he loved Israel. An Edomite is a brother, an Egyptian was a host, and their grandchildren may enter.

Then the camp. Because the LORD walks in the middle of it, it is to be kept holy, and Moses even gives instructions about a trowel to cover waste.

There is also mercy. A servant who has escaped from his master is not to be returned and not to be oppressed. A brother is not to be charged interest. A vow is to be paid, and a hungry traveler may eat grapes from a neighbor's vineyard, though not carry any away.

The rules for the assembly are not the last word in Scripture. Isaiah 56 speaks of foreigners and eunuchs who hold fast to the covenant, and the book of Ruth tells of a Moabite woman welcomed into Israel's story and into the line of David. The verse about an escaped servant stands out in the ancient world, and many readers have linked it to later arguments about slavery. Verse 17 uses a word that readers translate in more than one way.

Behind this chapter is a household where people are easily overlooked, and Moses keeps stopping to look at them. A man divorces his wife by writing a certificate and putting it in her hand. If she marries again and that marriage ends, her first husband may not take her back. Jesus will speak to this passage in the Gospels.

A newly married man is free from the army for a year, to cheer his wife. A millstone may not be taken as a pledge, for it takes a life in pledge. A lender must wait outside and let the poor man bring out his own pledge, and a cloak taken at dawn must be returned at sunset so he can sleep in it.

Wages of the poor are to be paid the same day, for he sets his heart on it. Children are not to die for their fathers. The foreigner, the fatherless and the widow are to be given justice, and the leftover sheaf, olives and grapes are theirs. Remember that you were a slave in Egypt.

Verses 1 to 4 do not command divorce but regulate a custom already in practice, and Jesus returns to them in Matthew 19 and Mark 10. Christians read his words in different ways. Verse 16 is often noted as a principle of individual responsibility, and Ezekiel 18 develops it. The gleaning rule is the background to the story of Ruth. Verse 9 refers to the account in Numbers 12.

The chapter opens in a courtroom. The judges justify the righteous and condemn the wicked, and if a beating is called for, it is limited to forty stripes, so that your brother is not degraded in your sight. Even in punishment there is a floor of dignity.

Then a brief line about work: you shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain. After it comes the law of the brother's widow. When a man dies with no son, his brother is to marry the widow so the name is not blotted out of Israel. If he refuses, she brings it to the elders, removes his sandal and spits in his face, and his house gets a new name.

Some verses are hard, including a harsh penalty in verses 11 and 12. Then the market is made a matter of honesty, with no heavy and light weights in the bag, since dishonest dealing is an abomination to the LORD.

The last words recall Amalek, who struck the weary stragglers and did not fear God.

The levirate law is shown at work in Genesis 38 and in the book of Ruth, and the Sadducees raise it with Jesus in Mark 12. Paul quotes the line about the ox in 1 Corinthians 9 and 1 Timothy 5, as a principle that workers deserve their keep. Verses 17 to 19 refer back to Exodus 17 and look forward to 1 Samuel 15. The command about Amalek is a hard text, and readers have long debated how to take it.

A farmer walks up to the place of worship with a basket of the first fruits of his ground. He hands it to the priest, who sets it before the altar, and then he says a short creed from memory. My father was a Syrian ready to perish. He went down to Egypt, few in number, and became a great nation. The Egyptians mistreated us, and we cried to the LORD, who heard our voice and saw our oppression and brought us out with a mighty hand.

So the offering is a story told out loud, and the joy of the harvest is shared with the Levite and the foreigner. Every third year the tithe goes to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. The worshiper declares that he has done as commanded and asks for the LORD's blessing.

The chapter ends with an exchange. Today you have declared that the LORD is your God, and today the LORD has declared that you are his own people.

This chapter closes the law section that began in chapter 12. The short creed in verses 5 to 10 is one of the oldest summaries of Israel's story, and many scholars treat it as an early confession of faith. The phrase my father was a Syrian refers to Jacob, who lived in Aram, as Genesis tells it, and some translations read the phrase differently. Jews still read this passage at Passover. The mutual declaration in verses 17 and 18 is the covenant in a few words.

On the day Israel crosses the Jordan, they are to set up great stones, coat them with plaster, and write all the words of this law on them very plainly. On Mount Ebal they will also build an altar of uncut stones, with no iron tool, and offer burnt offerings and peace offerings, and eat and rejoice before the LORD.

Moses and the Levitical priests then say, Be silent and listen, Israel. Today you have become the people of the LORD your God.

Half the tribes are to stand on Mount Gerizim to bless and half on Mount Ebal for the curse. The Levites speak the curses in a loud voice, and after each one all the people answer, Amen. The curses fall on secret idolatry, dishonoring parents, moving a landmark, leading the blind astray, denying justice to the foreigner, fatherless and widow, forbidden sexual acts, secret murder, taking a bribe to kill the innocent, and, last of all, anyone who does not uphold the words of this law by doing them.

Joshua 8 describes this ceremony being carried out at the same two mountains, near Shechem. Notice that the curses are about acts done in secret or hidden from a court, and about the vulnerable, so the people themselves agree with an Amen. Paul quotes verse 26 in Galatians 3, and Christians have read his argument in different ways. Chapter 28 continues with blessings and curses in more detail.

Two roads open in front of Israel, and Moses describes where each one goes. If they listen to the voice of the LORD, blessing will overtake them in city and field, in basket and kneading trough, in coming in and going out. Enemies will come at them one way and flee seven ways. The LORD will open his good treasure in the sky and make Israel the head, not the tail.

Then the other road, which takes far longer to tell. If they will not listen, the curses will overtake them just as surely: disease, drought, defeat, madness, and the loss of everything they build, plant and love. Their sky will be bronze and their earth iron.

The last section is the hardest in the book. A nation from far away will besiege their gates, and hunger will drive people to terrible things. They will be scattered among all peoples and sent back toward Egypt, with a trembling heart and no rest for the sole of the foot.

This is the end of the covenant speech of Moses, shaped like the blessings and curses at the close of ancient treaties. Many scholars think the vivid images of siege and exile later helped Israel understand the fall of Jerusalem and the exile to Babylon, which 2 Kings 25 describes. The chapter links blessing and obedience, and Job and Jesus in John 9 push against reading every misfortune as a direct punishment. These verses should never be used to blame victims.

Moses gathers everyone in the land of Moab for a covenant, in addition to the one made at Horeb. He calls them to look back at what their eyes have seen, the signs in Egypt, the forty years in the wilderness in which their clothes and sandals did not wear out. And yet the LORD has not given them a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.

The whole community stands there, leaders, little ones, wives and foreigners, from the one who cuts wood to the one who draws water. The covenant is not for them alone, but for those who are not here today.

Then a warning against the secret heart, a root that produces bitter poison, a person who hears the curse and blesses himself, saying, I shall have peace. Moses pictures future generations looking at a ruined land, like Sodom and Gomorrah, and asking why. The chapter ends with a famous line: the secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the revealed things belong to us and to our children.

The mention of foreigners and future generations shows that the covenant is meant to reach beyond the people standing there. Verse 4 is difficult, and readers have long asked how the LORD's gift and Israel's responsibility fit together. Many see the pictures of a ruined land as looking ahead to the exile, which Jeremiah 22 also describes. Verse 29 is often used for the limits of human knowledge and the call to act on what is clear.

After all the curses, Moses speaks of a way back. Suppose the blessing and the curse have both come, and Israel remembers them among the nations where the LORD has driven them. If they return to the LORD with all their heart and soul, he will release them from captivity, have compassion, and gather them even from the uttermost parts of the heavens. He will bring them to the land of their fathers.

The LORD himself will circumcise their hearts, so they love him and live.

Then Moses speaks of the commandment as something close. It is not in heaven, so that someone must climb up for it, and not beyond the sea, so that someone must cross over for it. The word is very near, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you may do it.

He ends with the choice. I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life, that you may live, you and your descendants, loving the LORD, obeying his voice and clinging to him.

The promise of return after exile is central to this chapter, and many scholars think it was especially meaningful to Israel in Babylon. Paul quotes verses 12 to 14 in Romans 10, applying them to the message about Christ, and Jewish readers have kept the passage as a statement about the closeness of the Torah. The circumcised heart appears also in Deuteronomy 10 and Jeremiah 31. Verse 19 is among the best known lines of the book.

I am one hundred twenty years old today. Moses stands before all Israel and says that he can no longer go out and come in, and that the LORD has told him he will not cross the Jordan. But the LORD himself will go over before them, and so will Joshua. He calls Joshua in front of everyone and tells him to be strong and courageous, for the LORD will not fail him nor forsake him.

Moses writes the law down and gives it to the priests and elders. Every seven years, at the feast of booths, it is to be read aloud to men, women, children and foreigners.

Then the LORD calls Moses and Joshua to the Tent of Meeting. He appears in a pillar of cloud and tells Moses, sadly, that the people will turn to other gods after his death. So Moses is to write a song and teach it to them, as a witness. The law is placed beside the ark, and Moses calls heaven and earth to witness against a people he knows are stiff-necked.

This chapter is a handover. Leadership passes from Moses to Joshua, and the law passes into writing and public reading. The call to be strong and courageous reappears at the opening of the book of Joshua. The LORD's words in verses 16 to 18 look ahead to the failures described in Judges and in the exile. Chapter 32 gives the song itself, and chapter 34 tells of Moses' death.

Moses sings. Let the heavens give ear, he begins, and his words fall like rain and dew on the tender grass. He calls the LORD the Rock, whose work is perfect and whose ways are just.

Then the song tells a story of care and betrayal. The LORD found Jacob in a desert land, in a howling wilderness, and kept him like the apple of his eye. Like an eagle stirring its nest, he spread his wings and carried his young. He gave them honey from the rock, oil, milk, wheat and wine. But Jeshurun grew fat and kicked, forgot the Rock who bore him, and ran to new gods.

The LORD answers with anger, and the song describes hunger, plague and the sword. Yet he holds back, so his enemies cannot boast. He declares that there is no god beside him, that he kills and makes alive, wounds and heals. The song ends in verse 43 with a call to rejoice and a promise of atonement for his land and people.

Then the LORD tells Moses to climb Mount Nebo and die there.

The song was meant to be learned and sung, as chapter 31 says. Jeshurun is a poetic name for Israel. Verse 8 is read in different ways, since ancient manuscripts differ on the number of the nations, and readers have long discussed it. Paul quotes verse 21 in Romans 10 and verse 35 in Romans 12, and verse 43 appears in Romans 15. The reason Moses may not enter the land, in verse 51, refers to the event at Meribah in Numbers 20.

Before he dies, Moses blesses the tribes. The scene is a goodbye. He begins with the LORD coming from Sinai like the dawn, with a fiery law at his right hand, and says that the LORD loves his people.

Then he turns to the tribes one by one. Reuben is to live and not die. Judah is asked to be brought in to his people, with the LORD as a help against his enemies. Levi is to teach Jacob the ordinances and put incense before the LORD. Benjamin is the beloved who dwells in safety. Joseph receives the precious things of heaven, earth and ancient hills.

Zebulun and Issachar are told to rejoice. Gad is a lioness, Dan a lion's cub, Naphtali is satisfied with favor, and Asher is blessed with children, with bars of iron and bronze and strength to match his days.

The last words are for all of Israel. There is no one like God. The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms. You are happy, Israel.

This blessing resembles the blessing of Jacob on his sons in Genesis 49, and the two are often compared. Simeon is not named here, and readers have long wondered why. The tribe of Levi, who were set apart for priestly service, is given a role in teaching the law. The poem looks ahead to a future in the land, and Moses speaks as a man who will not enter it. Verse 27 is often quoted for comfort.

Moses climbs from the plains of Moab to the top of Pisgah, opposite Jericho. There the LORD shows him the whole land, from Gilead to Dan, all Naphtali, Ephraim and Manasseh, all Judah to the Western Sea, the south and the valley of Jericho, the city of palm trees.

The LORD says, This is the land which I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. I have caused you to see it with your eyes, but you shall not go over there. It is a moment of grief and of promise together.

So Moses the servant of the LORD died there, according to the LORD's word. The LORD buried him in the valley in Moab, but no one knows where his tomb is to this day. He was one hundred twenty years old, and his eye was not dim, nor his strength gone.

Israel wept for him thirty days. Joshua, full of the spirit of wisdom, took up the work. The book ends with a tribute: no prophet since has been like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face.

This final chapter closes the five books of the Law, the Torah. Tradition links the writing of the Torah to Moses, and the account of his death shows that at least this ending was added by someone else, a point that readers and scholars have noted for centuries. The note that no prophet has risen like Moses fits well with Deuteronomy 18. Jude 9 mentions a dispute over his body. Joshua 1 continues the story.
